title: Cancer Genetics, Genetic Counselling and Nursing Management of Selected Cancers
introduction: Cancer fundamentally reflects a failure of tissue growth regulation driven by accumulated mutations in oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes, and DNA repair genes[cite: 457, 462]. Combining primary cancer prevention and family-history genetic counselling with specialized medical-surgical nursing care for breast cancer, leukemia, lymphoma, and colon cancer empowers nurses to protect survival and preserve patient quality of life[cite: 463, 469, 482, 489].
learningOutcomes: 8.1 Explain the relationship between heredity, aging, DNA mutations, oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes (including p53), and DNA repair genes in carcinogenesis[cite: 457, 458, 460, 461, 462].
8.2 Outline the eight evidence-based cancer prevention measures targeting lifestyle, viral, dietary, and occupational carcinogens[cite: 463, 464, 465].
8.3 Define genetic counselling, state the four values of family history, and identify the twelve genetic red flags[cite: 469, 470].

8.4 Apply prenatal risk assessment and management guidelines to X-linked Fragile X syndrome (FMR-1 repeat expansion, pre-mutation vs. full-mutation carriers, and reproductive counselling)[cite: 475, 476, 477, 478, 479].
8.5 Formulate comprehensive nursing management and quality-of-life care plans for patients with breast cancer, leukemia, lymphoma, and colon cancer[cite: 482, 485, 488, 489].

content.heading: Heredity, DNA Mutations, Oncogenes, Tumour Suppressor and DNA Repair Genes
content.body: Although 80%–90% of cancers occur in individuals without a family history—with hereditary conditions accounting for 10% or fewer of all cancer cases (including about 5% of breast cancers linked to inherited susceptibility genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2)—inherited mutations significantly raise lifetime susceptibility[cite: 457, 458]. Genetic testing should always be voluntary and paired with genetic counselling[cite: 458]. Cancer risk also rises steeply with aging as mutations accumulate (for example, a 75-year-old is 100 times more likely to develop colon cancer than a 25-year-old)[cite: 458]. Chemicals and radiation damage DNA, viruses insert their own genes, and heredity transmits susceptibility mutations within the DNA double helix (composed of adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine) via single-base errors, insertions, deletions, or rearrangements[cite: 458, 459]. Three key gene classes drive malignancy: (1) Oncogenes—mutated forms of normal proto-oncogenes (which encode growth factors, receptors, signalling enzymes, and transcription factors) that act like a stuck gas pedal, driving continuous hyperactive cell division[cite: 459, 460]; (2) Tumour suppressor genes—paired normal genes acting like brake pedals whose functional loss allows unchecked proliferation (inheriting one defective copy requires a second-copy mutation for cancer to arise); notably, the p53 protein halts growth in DNA-damaged cells and triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable[cite: 461]; and (3) DNA repair genes—genes that correct DNA duplication errors; inherited defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum (inability to repair UV skin damage, causing high skin cancer rates) and hereditary colon cancer[cite: 461, 462]. Malignant transformation requires releasing the brakes while activating accelerators, alongside mutations affecting carcinogen metabolism, cell cycle, senescence, apoptosis, and invasion—where tumours lose stop-growth receptors, amplify self-growth signals, and secrete cytokines and proteases that break down basement membranes and surrounding matrix to enter blood or lymphatic vessels[cite: 462].

content.heading: Cancer Prevention Strategies
content.body: Because carcinogens trigger most human cancers, prevention targets eight priority areas[cite: 463, 466]: (1) Avoid tobacco—the single most effective lifestyle decision, as tobacco causes roughly one in three cancer deaths, nearly all lung cancers, and cancers of the mouth, larynx, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, kidney, and bladder[cite: 463]; (2) Protect against excessive sunlight—avoiding intense sun, wearing protective clothing, and using sunscreen to reduce skin cancer and potentially lethal melanoma[cite: 463]; (3) Limit alcohol and tobacco together—excess alcohol raises mouth, throat, and oesophageal cancer risk roughly 6-fold alone, but combining heavy smoking and heavy drinking increases oesophageal cancer risk more than 40-fold[cite: 463, 464]; (4) Limit dietary fats and calories—reducing high-fat meat and excess calories lowers risk, especially for colon cancer[cite: 464]; (5) Consume fruits and vegetables—eating 5 to 9 servings daily strongly correlates with reduced cancer risk[cite: 464]; (6) Avoid cancer-causing viruses—limiting exposure to the 13 high-risk sexually transmitted HPV types (out of >100 HPV types) responsible for cervical cancer[cite: 464, 465]; (7) Avoid workplace carcinogens—preventing occupational exposures such as asbestos, which raises construction workers' cancer risk 10-fold[cite: 465]; and (8) Understand industrial pollution—while localized chemical exposure poses risks to workers and nearby residents, age-adjusted cancer rates over the past half-century indicate industrial pollution is not a primary driver of most cancers population-wide[cite: 465].

content.heading: Genetic Counselling: Family History Value and Twelve Red Flags
content.body: Genetic counselling advises patients and families at risk of an inherited disorder regarding the nature and consequences of the condition, probability of developing or transmitting it, and available management and family planning options[cite: 469]. A thorough family history delivers four core clinical values: informing diagnosis, promoting risk assessment, guiding management, and building rapport[cite: 469]. Effective family-history collection tools generate red flags and risk reports, offer decision-support algorithms, respect cultural and ethical considerations, support education, and integrate with electronic health records[cite: 470]. Clinicians screen pedigrees for twelve genetic red flags: (1) known or suspected genetic condition in relatives; (2) multiple affected relatives with the same or related disorders (suggesting autosomal dominant if an affected parent is present, recessive if neither parent is affected, X-linked if only males are affected, or complex traits if no clear Mendelian pattern exists); (3) earlier-than-expected age of onset; (4) intellectual disability; (5) diagnosis in the less-often-affected sex (such as male breast cancer); (6) multifocal or bilateral disease in paired organs (such as inherited bilateral vs. sporadic unilateral retinoblastoma); (7) one or more major malformations (e.g., heart defects, cleft lip/palate) or multiple minor malformations; (8) disease occurring despite a low-risk lifestyle or preventive measures; (9) prenatal or postnatal growth abnormalities (retardation, asymmetry, excess); (10) recurrent pregnancy losses (2 or more spontaneous miscarriages); (11) consanguinity (biologically related parents, raising autosomal recessive risk, distinct from first-degree incest); and (12) ethnic or geographic predisposition (e.g., sickle cell disease in African Americans, cystic fibrosis in Northern European Caucasians and Ashkenazi Jews—with geographic origin being more objective than ethnicity)[cite: 470, 471, 472, 473].

content.heading: Prenatal Risk Assessment and Fragile X Syndrome Case Application
content.body: Once red flags emerge, clinicians apply evidence-based prenatal guidelines (such as ACOG recommendations) illustrated by a 30-year-old woman (Anna) at 10 weeks' gestation whose brother (Harold) has intellectual disability (ID) and whose mother (Sarah) experienced menopause at age 32[cite: 473, 474, 475]. While 75% of ID causes are unknown, the three most common known causes are Down syndrome (usually sporadic, with relative risk rising significantly over age 35), Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (maternal alcohol exposure), and Fragile X syndrome—the most common inherited cause of ID (~1 in 4,000 males and 1 in 8,000 females)[cite: 474, 475, 476]. Fragile X is caused by an X-linked recessive CGG-trinucleotide repeat expansion on the FMR-1 gene: 55–200 repeats define pre-mutation carriers (normal cognition, 20%–22% risk of Primary Ovarian Insufficiency/menopause before age 40 in females, and late-onset tremors/ataxia mainly in males), whereas >200 repeats define full-mutation carriers (methylating FMR-1 and halting FMRP protein production)[cite: 475, 476, 477]. Affected individuals show mild-to-severe ID, long ears/face/jaw, loose joints, flat feet, behavioural/anxiety or attention challenges, speech/language delays (primarily in boys), and sensory sensitivities[cite: 477]. A carrier mother passes the mutation to 50% of sons (affected) and 50% of daughters (carriers); a carrier father passes it to 0% of sons and 100% of daughters[cite: 476, 477]. Per ACOG Committee Opinion #469, three immediate steps are taken: test both Anna and Harold simultaneously for FMR-1 (since results take 2–4 weeks), refer for genetic counselling (ensuring informed consent), and assess Anna's anxiety[cite: 478]. For a full-mutation female carrier (who typically avoids infertility but may face cognitive decline and anxiety/depression), follow-up includes early developmental assessment for her daughter, discussing reproductive options for future pregnancies (prenatal diagnosis, pre-implantation genetic diagnosis, egg donation, adoption), and encouraging family notification to siblings[cite: 478, 479].

content.heading: Nursing Management of Breast Cancer and Leukemia
content.body: Because breast cancer patients rarely have unpleasant symptoms at diagnosis, the news often causes shock, fear, anger, anxiety, denial, and depression (Weaver, 2009); nurses assess emotional readiness, encourage verbalizing fears, educate on treatment choices, and involve significant others with permission[cite: 482]. Preoperatively, nurses provide sufficient information for informed consent, monitor distress signs (tachycardia, muscle tension, insomnia, restlessness), explain surgical recovery, and teach turning, coughing, deep breathing, post-op exercises, and pain plans[cite: 483]. Postoperatively, nurses monitor vital signs half-hourly for the first 24 hours; inspect for bleeding, hematoma, and infection; manage post-mastectomy, bone, and neurologic pain (reassessing when analgesics are requested and 30–60 minutes after administration); restore arm function (semi-Fowler's position, affected arm elevated on pillows, flexion/extension); offer small desired meals and fluids; teach drain milking/stripping and measurement; prevent lymphedema (occurring in 15%–28% per McKenzie, 2012—via arm exercises, avoiding trauma, avoiding early post-op elastic bandages, and good nutrition); manage chemotherapy nausea/vomiting (~90% incidence—via prophylactic dexamethasone and serotonin antagonists, acupuncture, and relaxation); prepare for breast prosthesis fitting ~6 weeks post-op once edema resolves; manage fatigue, hot flashes, osteoporosis, and chemo brain; and address psychological, reproductive, and sexuality concerns[cite: 483, 484]. In Leukemia, treatment and prognosis depend on age, immunologic cell surface markers, and cytogenetics[cite: 485]. Nurses help families cope with abrupt sick-role losses, maximize physical functioning, offer hope that acute treatment side effects are temporary, advocate during complex treatment choices, monitor for remission or relapse, and educate patients/caregivers on maintenance chemotherapy, drug safety, self-care, and warning signs[cite: 485].

content.heading: Nursing Management of Lymphoma, Colon Cancer and Quality of Life
content.body: Lymphoma care (Hodgkin's and Non-Hodgkin's) is largely outpatient unless complications like infection or mediastinal-mass respiratory compromise arise[cite: 485]. Chemotherapy produces systemic side effects (myelosuppression, nausea, hair loss, infection), whereas radiation causes site-specific effects (e.g., abdominal radiation causes nausea and diarrhoea without alopecia), and both cause fatigue[cite: 485, 486]. Because immunosuppression and myelosuppression create high infection risk—and survivors face increased second malignancies—patient education emphasizes avoiding crowds, infected visitors (especially children with colds), and direct pet contact; frequent handwashing; prompt infection reporting; high-calorie, high-protein diets; sips of orange/grapefruit juice or ginger for nausea; ≥2 L fluid/day unless restricted; soft-toothbrush oral care without commercial mouthwashes; radiation skin care; and regular follow-up screening[cite: 486]. In Table 16.1 of the manual, Hodgkin vs. Non-Hodgkin features are contrasted as increasing vs. bimodal age, M:F 1.7:1 vs. 5:1, Stage 3–4 vs. 1–2, 15% vs. 25%–40% B symptoms, random vs. centripetal spread, leukemia common vs. rare, 80% vs. >95% nodal, 20% vs. 50% mediastinal, and 70% vs. 10% marrow involvement[cite: 487]. For Colon Cancer, nurses assess past risk factors (breast/cervical cancer, familial polyposis, villous/adenomatous polyps, IBD) and signs (pallor, cachexia, palpable abdominal mass, ascites, hepatomegaly, anaemia, guaiac-positive stool)[cite: 488]. Pre-op care covers physical preparation, colostomy/stoma education, intense emotional support, side-to-side positioning, and sitz bath positioning; post-op care monitors pain, anastomotic leakage, stoma prolapse, pulmonary complications, returning peristalsis, initial stool, ambulation on post-op day 1 to begin stoma self-care, aseptic IV care, handwashing, a high-fibre diet, and taking bowel medications only as prescribed[cite: 488, 489]. Quality of life (Ropka & Padilla, 2007; assessed via CDC HRQOL-4 and HRQOL-14) spans physical needs (weight loss, taste changes, altered bowel habits, stoma/fistula odours, sexual/erectile/ejaculatory dysfunction), psychological needs (anxiety, depression, body image, fertility), social restrictions, and family-history information needs[cite: 487, 489, 490].

inTextQuestions.question: Approximately what percentage of all cancer cases involve inherited hereditary conditions, and what happens to a patient with xeroderma pigmentosum?
inTextQuestions.answer: Hereditary conditions account for 10% or fewer of all cancer cases[cite: 457, 458]. A patient with xeroderma pigmentosum has an inherited defect in a DNA repair gene, preventing effective repair of sunlight-induced skin DNA damage and causing an abnormally high incidence of skin cancer[cite: 461, 462].

inTextQuestions.question: How much does the risk of oesophageal cancer increase in individuals who are both heavy smokers and heavy drinkers compared to non-smokers/non-drinkers?
inTextQuestions.answer: While heavy smoking or heavy drinking alone increases oesophageal cancer risk roughly 6-fold, combining both increases the risk more than 40-fold[cite: 464].

inTextQuestions.question: In the prenatal genetic counselling case, why did ACOG Opinion #469 recommend testing both Anna and her brother Harold for the FMR-1 gene simultaneously rather than sequentially?
inTextQuestions.answer: Because FMR-1 testing takes 2 to 4 weeks for results; testing Harold first and waiting before testing Anna could take two months or more, and time is critical since Anna is already 10 weeks pregnant[cite: 478].

inTextQuestions.question: Postoperatively after breast cancer surgery, how frequently should vital signs be monitored during the first 24 hours, and when is a breast prosthesis typically fitted?
inTextQuestions.answer: Vital signs should be monitored half-hourly for the first 24 hours, and a breast prosthesis is usually fitted about 6 weeks after surgery once wounds are healing well and postoperative edema has resolved[cite: 483, 484].

saqs.question: Compare oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes (including p53), and DNA repair genes in the molecular development of cancer.
saqs.answer: Oncogenes are mutated proto-oncogenes that produce altered or excessive growth-signalling proteins—acting like a stuck gas pedal driving constant division[cite: 460]. Tumour suppressor genes are paired normal genes acting like brake pedals whose loss or mutation of both copies permits uncontrolled growth; p53 specifically halts division in DNA-damaged cells and initiates apoptosis if damage is irreparable[cite: 461]. DNA repair genes correct DNA replication errors, and mutations in them allow subsequent mutations to accumulate rapidly[cite: 461].

saqs.question: List six evidence-based measures individuals can take to prevent cancer.
saqs.answer: 1. Avoid all forms of tobacco (the single most effective step)[cite: 463]; 2. Protect skin from excessive ultraviolet sunlight with sunscreen and clothing[cite: 463]; 3. Limit alcohol intake and avoid combining alcohol with tobacco[cite: 463, 464]; 4. Limit dietary fats and excess calories[cite: 464]; 5. Consume 5 to 9 servings of fruits and vegetables daily[cite: 464]; and 6. Avoid cancer-associated viruses (such as high-risk HPV) and workplace carcinogens like asbestos[cite: 464, 465].

saqs.question: State the four clinical values of taking a family history in genetic counselling and list six genetic red flags.
saqs.answer: The four values are informing diagnosis, promoting risk assessment, guiding management, and building rapport[cite: 469, 480]. Six genetic red flags include: (1) family history of a known or suspected genetic condition, (2) multiple affected family members with the same/related disorders, (3) earlier-than-expected age of onset, (4) intellectual disability, (5) multifocal or bilateral occurrence in paired organs (or diagnosis in the less-often-affected sex), and (6) recurrent pregnancy losses (2+), major malformations, consanguinity, or ethnic/geographic predisposition[cite: 470].

saqs.question: Differentiate pre-mutation and full-mutation Fragile X (FMR-1) carriers in terms of CGG repeat counts and clinical symptoms in males and females.
saqs.answer: Pre-mutation carriers have 55–200 CGG repeats and typically normal cognition; female pre-mutation carriers have a 20%–22% risk of Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (menopause before age 40), and carriers (mostly males) risk late-onset tremors/ataxia[cite: 475, 476, 477]. Full-mutation carriers have over 200 repeats, causing FMR-1 methylation and loss of FMRP protein: full-mutation males exhibit Fragile X syndrome symptoms, whereas full-mutation females generally have no fertility issues and mostly normal cognition (though possible cognitive decline) but higher rates of anxiety and depression[cite: 476, 478, 479].

saqs.question: Outline key postoperative nursing care measures for a patient following breast cancer surgery and key infection-prevention teaching points for a patient with lymphoma.
saqs.answer: Postoperative breast cancer care includes half-hourly vital signs for 24 hours, assessing bleeding/hematoma/infection, pain reassessment 30–60 minutes after analgesics, elevating the affected arm on pillows in semi-Fowler's with exercises, drain care, lymphedema prevention (avoiding trauma and early elastic bandages), antiemetics for chemotherapy, and prosthesis guidance at ~6 weeks[cite: 483, 484]. Lymphoma infection-prevention teaching includes avoiding crowds, infected visitors (especially children with colds), and direct pet contact, frequent handwashing, reporting any infection immediately, soft-toothbrush mouth care (avoiding commercial mouthwashes), drinking ≥2 L fluid/day, and eating a high-calorie, high-protein diet[cite: 486].
